<!-- What is established about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as it stands now, grouped by area: each entry the fact, its source and its test. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `FACTS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. -->

# Facts on record

## Execution model

- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet Rule for Functional Methods) and F-145 (uncovered abstract methods and `override`). The phases and where the two paths part: the skill's "How a program runs". Detail: `explorations/repo-internals.md`, "The two worlds".
- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.
- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. No share of the 0.74 s is measured.
- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team left two separate traces for unboxing. The plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java` lists what to unbox: a primitive, a singleton object, unboxed fields, and a `comprises` clause whose types are unboxable; it says nothing of the loader or of instantiations. The loader has an empty "expando" stub (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`). A loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.
- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, the arguments of a function call and of a dotted method call fork where the analyzer marked the argument tuple (`CodeGen.evalArg`; joins: F-350); it counts no call in the prelude's files (row 982) or of a function declared later in the file (row 987). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits a `ZZ32` range into chunks of at most 16 elements (F-350), and a range with a stride down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1498-1585`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.
- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129). Under walk, `Vector` and `Matrix` take their sizes from an array built at run time: `f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` takes `s` from `array[\RR64\](3)`, and overloads on `Vector` and `Matrix` dispatch by rank (row 214). The array-type syntax `T[n]` with a `nat` parameter does not unify with such an array, "Cannot unify … with ArrayType", where `T[3]` with a literal size does (row 23). Walk matches sizes at dispatch. A mismatch, such as a `DOT`, the library's inner product, of a 2×3 matrix by a 2×3 matrix, whose inner sizes differ, is a `ProgramError`, "Failed to find any matching overload", that no `catch` takes (row 254). Source: `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:96`.
- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). Both paths stop at a syntax error at `excludes`, since an object has no `excludes` clause (measured: `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, both report `T is undefined` at the `T` of the `extends` clause: a `where` clause on an object binds no type variable of its `extends` clause, as row 17 holds for a trait. Today's specification refuses the form in any case, by instantiation exclusion, and marks it "Not allowed" beside the parametric `Nothing[\T\]` that the interpreter's library writes (F-167). P-90 still calls the bare `Nothing` future work that waits for such `where` clauses, not tried before then. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-maybe/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is generated. The code generator names a reference to an exported declaration after the api, and the declaring class after the component. The link step rewrites such a reference to the component only when the repository names it, so files compiled one by one, without `fortress link`, die with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The missing step is the repository's: finding the component that exports the api. The report names two repairs, neither built: the repository could search the source path for that component, or the code generator could emit api-named forwarders, for which three comments in `CodeGen.java` leave a place. Walk and `fortress link` need the first. Workaround: name the api after its component. Gated by the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test` (row 320). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`, "The measurement that separates them".
- F-23 **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it.** The parser's `createSpan` trims back over spaces only, and a declaration that ends in `end` is unaffected (row 359). So a comment-only library edit can change the syntax tree, and a before-and-after comparison of parse trees or diagnostics maps positions back first. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 6, D1.
- F-24 **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees.** It throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object, as `Int.overflow()` does for `IntegerOverflow` (F-132; row 347, fixed). A native bound to a helper of `nativeHelpers/` raises the library's own exception where the helper raises a class of the compiled prelude, such as `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero`, so `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` (F-299, F-306, F-308, F-312). Any other Java exception of a native becomes a `ProgramError`, which no `catch` takes. Gated by the `overflows(...)` assertions of `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`, and for a helper by `tests/NativeHelperRaiseWalk.fss` and, for each of the five types, `tests/<type>DivisionByZeroWalk.fss` and `tests/<type>RemainderByZeroWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` section 4.1.
- F-25 **On the compiled path, the class loader loads each class under the JDK's class-loading lock, so the first load of an instantiation's class is safe on four threads at once.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` holds `getClassLoadingLock(name)` for the whole load, as the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` does. Without the lock, two threads that first loaded such classes at the same time could race, and the run died with a `NullPointerException` (row 417, fixed). The test `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` calls the generic overload `f[\T\](v: Vt[\T\])` at eight instantiations, `Vt[\A1\]` to `Vt[\A8\]`, from a parallel `for` loop of 800 iterations. Observed: at four threads it failed 5 runs of 5 before the lock, and passed 5 of 5 after. It is one of the gate's atomic runs, which run each program at four threads (`gate.md`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 (the runs) and 12 (why this lock).
- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** It builds P-45, the choice among overloads by declared parameter types, under walk. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains). If the chosen declaration is generic and its instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts the argument and dispatches the converted arguments again, so the most specific declaration for the converted values runs. In two cases walk keeps the chosen instance, with no second dispatch: an overloaded dotted method, and a position whose conversion `Coercions.coercionFor` does not find, such as a tuple converted element by element. Two generic overloads whose static parameters agree in name, kind and bounds share one symbolic instance, even if their `where` clauses differ; no test or library declaration has such a pair (row 478). Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.1, 5.2 (the second dispatch) and 5.5 (the symbolic instance).
- F-27 **Walk's load check reads again two kinds of overload pair that its parameter-by-parameter check refuses, and accepts those that pass: a generic declaration beside a plain one, read on their declared domains, and two plain top-level functions, not methods, whose overlap other declarations cover through `comprises` clauses.** To test a cover, the check cuts the overlap of the two domains, position by position, into parts by the `comprises` clauses. Each combination of parts must lie inside the domain of one declaration without static parameters that lies below both. So several such declarations may together cover the overlap. A search that does not settle refuses. A generic declaration beside a plain one passes where one declared domain lies strictly inside the other and the inner one's return type lies below the outer one's. Where neither lies inside the other, the pair needs the same cover, or declared domains that exclude each other read whole (F-258, exclusion over the whole parameter type). Equal declared domains are refused. ## Which tier runs what

- Give each worker its tier's alias: `model: 'opus'`, `'sonnet'` or `'fable'`. Write no identifier that an alias resolves to.
- Use Sonnet only for archaeology and to fetch exact words, never for a judgement or a summary. Have an Opus worker turn the evidence into a report, and condense a long report into a summary or the exact quotes that you need.
- To recheck a point at its source, have a fresh Sonnet scout fetch the exact words from the transcript or the commits. Have an Opus worker set them against the curator's memory and against the report, entry or summary that it differs from. Until then, state neither side as right, and take no step that rests on the point until the recheck ends.
- Run an Opus worker that writes or condenses a long report at extra high effort, `xhigh`: the Agent tool's `effort` option, `agent()`'s `opts.effort`, or `--effort xhigh` on a headless session's command line.
- Run every writer on Opus: of skill text, of record entries, and of each longer report or page for the curator, also when this session runs on Fable. Fable writes no text that goes as written into the record, since its compressed register degrades the reasoning. A Fable worker may give corrections to a text that Opus writes, and Opus words them into the text. A Fable review may edit a batch record in place.
- The rules on Fable's text hold while Fable is at version 5.1. When this session runs on Fable, `explorations/coordinator/tools/model-now.sh` prints its version.
- Take a cross-area question in two steps. First, Opus workers gather cited evidence or a list of ways. Then, if neither the record nor the three principles (`SKILL.md`) settle it, run a Fable judgement, sparingly. If the fork stays consequential, put it to the curator as an ask.
- Four kinds of Fable work have a go in advance: the Fable judgement on a cross-area question, a judge's second ruling in a batch, the Fable review of each batch record, and the comparison of a rewritten skill part with the version that the curator approved. Ask first for any other Fable worker, such as one on your own conduct, one whose answer would reverse the curator's decision, or a Fable and an Opus worker run apart on one question.
- If you start a headless session on a tier other than Opus or Fable, set `FORTRESS_HEADLESS=1` in its environment. Otherwise the model check's alarm stops its work (`SKILL.md`, "The boot"). Today only the baseline interview does so.
- Start every headless session with `--session-id` and a new UUID. Without it, the session writes into your own transcript, where its prompts read as the curator's messages.
- A Fable token also uses the all-models limits, at three to four times an Opus token's share of the session limit.

Source: the one-time strip of `.tex` line numbers, commit `dc0eee2fe`. The `fortress-repo` skill gives the rule to workers (`tests-writing.md`, "Names, comments, citations").
192	- F-113 **A harness run against another build's classes must point `FORTRESS_CACHES` at that build's caches as well as passing `-Dfortress.caches`.** A `.test` file's `run` step is a separate `bin/fortress run`, whose class path comes from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. Without it, the run fails "Could not load ... Resource not found". The run step runs no checker code, so the tree's own classes serve it. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-return-type-rule/REPORT.md` section 4; the `fortress-repo` skill's `worktrees.md`.
193	- F-114 **`ant testSpecData` runs 130 of the specification's 133 extracted examples under walk, as a gate step, and all 130 pass.** `SpecDataJUTest` runs `SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries` and `advanced`, not `library/`'s three, and `testFast` excludes it. It builds P-124. Five examples write no static argument on a generic big operator whose bound mentions its static parameter, and they pass only because walk leaves that parameter open (F-143; row 424, fixed). The count and the time: the last landed gate's `summary.txt`.
194	- F-203 **`explorations/experiment/env.sh` sets up a shell for the gate's runners, and sets `FORTRESS_HOME` from its own place in the tree.** It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` two folders above itself, replacing any value that the shell had (`env.sh:4`), so sourcing another tree's `env.sh` runs that tree's code. It also sets the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` and `JAVA_FLAGS`, and unsets `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`. It deletes a `/tmp/fortress*rats` parser folder only if nothing in it was written for an hour and every running `java` process started after its last write, so sourcing it does not break a live run. The compile ladder's drivers source it: `compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh` and its copy in `baseline-2026-09-19/`, and the two that the gate's ladder regression runs, `repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh` and `baseline-2026-09-19/microgpt-phase.sh`. Each of these sets its own `JAVA_FLAGS` after it. `experiment/setup.sh` sources it too. `microgpt-phase.sh` names the main tree's `env.sh` by its absolute path; the gate rewrites that path in its copy (the `fortress-repo` skill's `gate.md`, "The ladder regression"). The count stage's and the distance stage's `run.sh` do not source it: their headers tell the caller to source it first. A worker does not source it. It starts each Bash call with the `fortress-repo` skill's setup lines, which give the same settings (`build-and-caches.md`, "Setting up each call"). Evidence: read in the scripts; the deletion rule also in `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` section 4.
195	- F-234 **A Fortress command that a worker types itself (`bin/fortress`, `harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh`, or `java` of a Fortress main class) starts a fresh JVM, and that start costs too little to pay for a resident compiler.** A resident compiler is a background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did. The suites start one JVM for each test class, and one for each of `testSystem`'s four shards, not one for each test: the harness runs each test file inside its JVM. Only a compiled test's run step and a `.sh` test, such as `tests/concurrentPrinting.sh`, start another process. In one measurement over 267 worker transcripts, the one-off commands took 17.5 % of the wall time of the workers' shell commands, and the suites, builds and stages 47.8 %. Over the workers' whole running time, the one-off commands took 6.4 % (11.6 % if every wait that the measurement could not tie to a run was theirs). Removing their JVM start-up would save at most 1.8 % (P-150: no resident compiler is built). What runs inside the suites and the stages was not measured. Detail: `coordinator/process-engineering/fresh-jvm-commands.md`, "Summary", "What a resident compiler could save, at most" and "Decisions not taken".
196	- F-283 **The 52 programs of the team's `DemoTests` reach their end under walk.** Run one at a time from `ProjectFortress/demos`, each exits 0 and prints no "fail", within a 600 s limit and on an empty input, with `wordcount2` run from the tree's root and `tennisRanking` given the three files of `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/tests/unit_tests/FileTests.java:809-818`. The demos run in no suite, so a batch that changes walk or its library runs them again (P-79). `Generator2Demo` draws its arrays by `random`, so a product of them can overflow in `PROD`, and one such `IntegerOverflow` stop in a run is not a regression (row 986). The compiled checker still refuses `trips.fss` (row 817). No gated test: the command is the driver in `compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md` section 13, and its output on the code that `4445d848b` committed is 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. Detail: the same report, section 3; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-27/REPAIR-review.md`, section 2.

It does not read the `@@TC COMPONENT-CRASH` lines that `tools/distance/shadow-patch.py:111-113` prints. Test: `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/test_classify.py`, `Readings`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-list-imports/REPORT.md`, sections 1 and 2.
198	- F-354 **Two compiles of one source by different builds of the compiler need not give the same bytes, so a comparison of jars cannot show that a change left the compiled code as it was.** The code generator writes a class's methods and a dispatch method's tests in an order that follows the JVM's identity hashes (row 996). Two cold compiles of the prelude by one build give equal classes, 590 of 590, because the default identity hash is the same sequence in each run. Under another hash mode 18 of `CompilerBuiltin`'s 312 classes differ: the same methods in another order. So the tests, not the bytes, show that a change of the compiler left the prelude undisturbed, and a result that depends on the order can come and go between builds, as the choice between two copies of one method does (row 990). Measured once, on `832f7d0d91`'s code. Detail: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/probe-y.md`, "6. A finding beside the question: the prelude's jars change with any change of the compiler".

200	
201	- F-117 **A compiled mutable variable's cell holds the language's top type, so a mutable variable of arrow type compiles and runs.** The cell holds `fortress.AnyType.Any`, not `FValue`, because a compiled closure is not an `FValue`. The cell's gated tests, `compiler_tests/AtomicTopLevel*Var` and `MutableTopLevelVarInLoop`, run no variable of arrow type. Detail: `compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 4.
202	- F-118 **A numeral's value reaches the compiled code intact, and the compiled path prints a large `NN32` or `NN64` value unsigned.** A numeral that no place types becomes its default through that type's own coercion, which the checker inserts (`Functionals.scala`, `defaultNumeral`); only a numeral that the checker leaves without a coercion reaches the code generator's fallback, a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by exact bit length (`CodeGen.java`, `forIntLiteralExpr`), and which numerals do is not measured. A folded constant that the coercion desugarer types at a library number type is that type's constant (F-340), and a numeral as written at a number type is its type's coercion folded to a constant or made once for the place (F-347). So on the compiled path `4294967295` and `18446744073709551615` keep their values, as under walk, where they are a `ZZ64` and a `ZZ` (F-74, F-341); an untyped binding of the second is a `ZZ`, its default (F-342). Gated, for the numerals at `ZZ`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, by `compiler_tests/IntLiteralWrapRepairR2`. Detail: `compile-ladder/repair-r2-literal-wrap/REPORT.md`, "The failure-mode question"; `compile-ladder/rung-static-numerals/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why".

Either it returns a type parameter of its own that is the whole type of at least one of its parameters and appears in no other parameter type than those at positions where the outer one's parameter type is that returned type parameter; or, at such a position, it has an object type below which its return type lies. Otherwise walk refuses the pair, "fails the Return Type Rule" (F-257). With `trait Shape`, `trait Round extends Shape` and `object Circle extends Round`, it refuses `f[\T extends Shape\](x: T, y: T): T` beside `f[\U extends Round\](x: U, y: Round): Round`, and `f[\T extends Shape\](x: T): Box[\T\]` beside `f[\U extends Round\](x: U): Box[\U\]`; the compiled checker refuses both too. Gated by `tests/GenericReturnRuleOuterParamWalk` and `GenericReturnRuleInvariantWalk` (refused) and `GenericReturnRuleHoldsWalk` (load and dispatch). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-generic-pairs/SKEPTIC.md` section 2.
249	- F-280 **The library's `=/=` over `Any` and its three-argument `assert` see a value's own `=` only through a `FortressLibrary` trait, so `List` extends `Equality[\List[\E\]\]`.** Under walk they call `=` in `FortressLibrary`'s scope (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:98`, `:308`). A type's own `=` reaches them only where it implements a `FortressLibrary` trait's `=`, such as `Equality`'s; otherwise they compare by identity (row 807). A type that extends `Equality` reaches `Equality`'s own `=/=` before the one over `Any`: the negation of its `=` (`:102`; F-366). `List` extends `Equality[\List[\E\]\]` outside its conditional order (`Library/List.fsi:67`), so a list's `=` stays element by element there whatever the condition. Tests: `XXXNotEqualOwnEquality`, `ListEqualityElementwise`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-slices-list-equality/REPORT.md`, sections 1 and 2.
250	- F-304 **On both paths a numeral with a radix point becomes its `RR64` or `RR32` by one rounding of its exact value.** The compiled `CodeGen.forFloatLiteralExpr` rounds the exact quotient once (`roundToDouble`, `roundToFloat`; F-340); walk rounds once through `simpleDoubleArith.numeralToDouble` and `numeralToFloat` (F-79). The specification asks "at most one floating-point rounding error" (`basic/expressions/literals.tex`, "Literals"). Test: `compiler_tests/FloatNumeralOneRounding.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-natives-float/REPORT.md`, "Defects, each with its home".
251	- F-305 **`CHOOSE` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` names its helper on both paths, and the helper is exact, raises `IntegerOverflow` where the binomial coefficient does not fit, and shares no state between calls.** It builds P-73. Trait `ZZ32`'s and trait `ZZ64`'s `CHOOSE` name `simpleIntArith.intOverflowingChoose` and `simpleLongArith.longOverflowingChoose` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:845`, `:954`), which the compiler's prelude binds too, `NN32`'s compiled `CHOOSE` through the `ZZ64` helper; `NN32`'s binding in the one library names `simpleUnsignedIntArith.unsignedIntOverflowingChoose` through the `NN32` transfer (F-313). Past their safe-bound tables every coefficient overflows, from `34 CHOOSE 17` on `ZZ32` and `68 CHOOSE 34` on `ZZ64`, and the helpers raise `IntegerOverflow` there (`nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.java:222-225`, `simpleLongArith.java:200-203`); each slow-path call has its own scratch array (`simpleIntArith.java:174-175`, `simpleLongArith.java:153-154`), so calls in parallel no longer corrupt each other. Swept against the exact value, 64,649,240 `ZZ64` pairs and 6,023,925 `ZZ32` pairs give walk's glue arithmetic. Test: `tests/ChooseHelperWalk.fss`, `tests/ChooseHelperZZ64Walk.fss`, `compiler_tests/ChooseHelperCompiled`, `compiler_tests/ChooseHelperZZ64Compiled`, `compiler_tests/ChooseTableCompiledRungE`; the guards `tests/ChooseZZ32Walk.fss` and `tests/ChooseZZ64Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-natives-choose/REPORT.md`, sections 1, 2 and 5.
252	- F-316 **Under walk, `GCD` and `LCM` are nonnegative, `0 LCM 0` is 0, and on the four fixed widths `n CHOOSE k` answers 0 for `k < 0` or `k > n`.** `GCD` and `LCM` hold this on the four fixed widths and on `ZZ`. On `ZZ`, `CHOOSE` answers 1 for `k < 0` or `k > n`, where the specification gives 0 (row 887, `tests/XXXChooseZZOutOfRangeWalk.fss`). A `GCD`, `LCM` or `CHOOSE` result that its type cannot hold, such as a fixed width's `MIN GCD 0`, raises `IntegerOverflow` (F-132). `LCM` carries no sign, so code that takes a direction from it must compute the sign itself. The team's `tests/RangePrototype.fss` does so with `(a DIV (a GCD b)) DOT b`, `DOT` being multiplication. The library's ranges do not depend on that sign. Gated by `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss` for `GCD` and `LCM` (rows 334 and 385, fixed), and by `tests/PowChooseLcmRungE.fss` for `CHOOSE` (row 337, fixed). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` sections 4.2 and 7.
253	- F-318 **Under walk, the load check reads an own generic beside a functional method of a generic trait on their declared domains, `self` of a self-typed trait read as `C[\X\] & X` in the exclusion test.** It builds P-157 and P-152. Where the parameter-by-parameter check refuses an own generic function beside a functional method of a generic trait that declares no static parameters of its own, walk reads the pair as two own generics (`genericPairValid`), the trait's static parameters standing for the method's own; in `domainsExcludeTogether`'s meet, the self parameter of a trait self-typed directly (its parameter `X` bounded by the trait at `X`, no `comprises` clause or one that lists only `...`) excludes a type where the trait's instance or `X` does (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java`, `validOnDeclaredDomains`, `traitMethodPairValid`, `selfTypeParameter`). So a program's generic operators between an array of a number type and a number, beside a self-typed additive group's own, load and run as on the compiled path, and with `Number`'s `comprises` clause removed, in a scratch copy before F-324 removed it from the library, walk loads and runs `BooleanOps`, `ArrayScalarExtension`, `ArrayOperatorsBesideLibrary` and `extendNumber`. A trait self-typed through another self-typed trait, and a method with static parameters of its own, are not read so and keep the refusal. Walk applies no extender rule of P-146, so an object that extends a self-typed trait at a type it is not a subtype of now loads and runs one of two fitting declarations (row 893); the checker refuses a generic function more specific than such a method that walk loads (row 894). Gated by `tests/ExclusionVectorScalarWalk`, `ExclusionArrayScalarLibraryShapeWalk`, `GenericBesideTraitMethodInsideWalk` and `GenericInsideTraitMethodWalk` (load and dispatch), and the refusals `ExclusionVectorScalarOverlapWalk` and `GenericInsideTraitMethodReturnRuleWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-vector-scalar/REPORT.md` sections 1, 2 and 4.
254	- F-324 **The one library's `Number` declares nothing; each number type declares its own `asFloat` and an `=` at each number type it coerces from or into.** It builds P-160's second step and P-165. `Number`'s `comprises` clause, `asFloat`, `=` and `exactValue` are struck (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:381-382`, `.fsi:289-290`); the nine types declare `asFloat` in their apis; 42 declarations give a pair of `=` for each of the 21 coercions, so two numbers of different types compare by value where a coercion joins them, and otherwise by the fallback `a SEQV b` or a written `asFloat(x) = y`; the vector norm is declared at each of the eight types; the reflective generator chooses among the five former listed types. A program's own number type compares by its own `=` or by the fallback. Gated by `tests/NumberOwnTypeNoAsFloatWalk`, `NumberEqualityOwnTypeWalk`, `NumberMixedEqualityWalk`, `VectorNormElementTypesWalk`, `NumberOwnTypeArrayWalk`, `NumberOpenTraitPlusBesideArrayWalk` and the team's `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-number-open/REPORT.md`.
255	- F-326 **Both paths answer `SEQV` by the specification's rule: values of different types never equivalent, value objects of one type field by field, floats by their bits, reference objects and strings only with themselves.** Walk in its value classes and `FTypeObject`'s field list; the compiled path in `equality.sEquiv`, which reads a `value` object by the mark `runtimeValues.ValueObjectMark` that the code generator adds to its class, and compares tuples element by element. Until the switch-over a compiled `===` reaches the prelude's family first, which answers `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64` values, strings and booleans by `=` (P-38, row 908). Under walk a float numeral bound to `RR64` converts there, so it is `SEQV` a computed `RR64` of the same bits (F-341), and two string literals of one text are one object on both paths (F-343); a tuple of four or more compares by `SEQV` (row 923). Tests: `tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleWalk.fss`, `tests/ValueObjectCC64Walk.fss`, `compiler_tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleCompiled.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-seqv-meaning/REPORT.md`.

- F-112 **The test corpora cite the specification by file and section, never by line.** A test names the heading of the section that it cites. In the library chapters, it names the trait or method entry too. A rung that renames or removes a cited section updates the citation in the same commit. No test comment names a `.tex` file with a line number: `grep -rnE '\.tex:[0-9]+'` over `ProjectFortress/tests`, `compiler_tests`, `library_tests`, `other_compiler_tests` and `parser_tests` prints nothing; one bare `:400-401` stays after the section that `compiler_tests/IntLiteralWrapRepairR2.fss:12-14` cites, left as it was. Source: the one-time strip of `.tex` line numbers, commit `dc0eee2fe`. The `fortress-repo` skill gives the rule to workers (`tests-writing.md`, "Names, comments, citations").
- F-113 **A harness run against another build's classes must point `FORTRESS_CACHES` at that build's caches as well as passing `-Dfortress.caches`.** A `.test` file's `run` step is a separate `bin/fortress run`, whose class path comes from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. Without it, the run fails "Could not load ... Resource not found". The run step runs no checker code, so the tree's own classes serve it. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-return-type-rule/REPORT.md` section 4; the `fortress-repo` skill's `worktrees.md`.
- F-114 **`ant testSpecData` runs 130 of the specification's 133 extracted examples under walk, as a gate step, and all 130 pass.** `SpecDataJUTest` runs `SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries` and `advanced`, not `library/`'s three, and `testFast` excludes it. It builds P-124. Five examples write no static argument on a generic big operator whose bound mentions its static parameter, and they pass only because walk leaves that parameter open (F-143; row 424, fixed). The count and the time: the last landed gate's `summary.txt`.
- F-203 **`explorations/experiment/env.sh` sets up a shell for the gate's runners, and sets `FORTRESS_HOME` from its own place in the tree.** It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` two folders above itself, replacing any value that the shell had (`env.sh:4`), so sourcing another tree's `env.sh` runs that tree's code. It also sets the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` and `JAVA_FLAGS`, and unsets `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`. It deletes a `/tmp/fortress*rats` parser folder only if nothing in it was written for an hour and every running `java` process started after its last write, so sourcing it does not break a live run. The compile ladder's drivers source it: `compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh` and its copy in `baseline-2026-09-19/`, and the two that the gate's ladder regression runs, `repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh` and `baseline-2026-09-19/microgpt-phase.sh`. Each of these sets its own `JAVA_FLAGS` after it. `experiment/setup.sh` sources it too. `microgpt-phase.sh` names the main tree's `env.sh` by its absolute path; the gate rewrites that path in its copy (the `fortress-repo` skill's `gate.md`, "The ladder regression"). The count stage's and the distance stage's `run.sh` do not source it: their headers tell the caller to source it first. A worker does not source it. It starts each Bash call with the `fortress-repo` skill's setup lines, which give the same settings (`build-and-caches.md`, "Setting up each call"). Evidence: read in the scripts; the deletion rule also in `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` section 4.
- F-234 **A Fortress command that a worker types itself (`bin/fortress`, `harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh`, or `java` of a Fortress main class) starts a fresh JVM, and that start costs too little to pay for a resident compiler.** A resident compiler is a background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did. The suites start one JVM for each test class, and one for each of `testSystem`'s four shards, not one for each test: the harness runs each test file inside its JVM. Only a compiled test's run step and a `.sh` test, such as `tests/concurrentPrinting.sh`, start another process. In one measurement over 267 worker transcripts, the one-off commands took 17.5 % of the wall time of the workers' shell commands, and the suites, builds and stages 47.8 %. Over the workers' whole running time, the one-off commands took 6.4 % (11.6 % if every wait that the measurement could not tie to a run was theirs). Removing their JVM start-up would save at most 1.8 % (P-150: no resident compiler is built). What runs inside the suites and the stages was not measured. Detail: `coordinator/process-engineering/fresh-jvm-commands.md`, "Summary", "What a resident compiler could save, at most" and "Decisions not taken".
- F-283 **The 52 programs of the team's `DemoTests` reach their end under walk.** Run one at a time from `ProjectFortress/demos`, each exits 0 and prints no "fail", within a 600 s limit and on an empty input, with `wordcount2` run from the tree's root and `tennisRanking` given the three files of `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/tests/unit_tests/FileTests.java:809-818`. The demos run in no suite, so a batch that changes walk or its library runs them again (P-79). `Generator2Demo` draws its arrays by `random`, so a product of them can overflow in `PROD`, and one such `IntegerOverflow` stop in a run is not a regression (row 986). The compiled checker still refuses `trips.fss` (row 817). No gated test: the command is the driver in `compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md` section 13, and its output on the code that `4445d848b` committed is 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. Detail: the same report, section 3; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-27/REPAIR-review.md`, section 2.
- F-295 **The distance stage counts each api's own errors and crashes, so an error in an api that only a later target checks cannot hide.** `table.py` turns `#total` into `none:` for an api whose `@@TC API` line gives `errors=` above 0 and that printed no `@@SC` line of its own, naming it with its count, and turns an `@@TC API-CRASH` line into a `#crash` row of kind `api` (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/table.py:54`, `:61-67`, `:94-104`). It does not read the `@@TC COMPONENT-CRASH` lines that `tools/distance/shadow-patch.py:111-113` prints. Test: `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/test_classify.py`, `Readings`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-list-imports/REPORT.md`, sections 1 and 2.
- F-354 **Two compiles of one source by different builds of the compiler need not give the same bytes, so a comparison of jars cannot show that a change left the compiled code as it was.** The code generator writes a class's methods and a dispatch method's tests in an order that follows the JVM's identity hashes (row 996). Two cold compiles of the prelude by one build give equal classes, 590 of 590, because the default identity hash is the same sequence in each run. Under another hash mode 18 of `CompilerBuiltin`'s 312 classes differ: the same methods in another order. So the tests, not the bytes, show that a change of the compiler left the prelude undisturbed, and a result that depends on the order can come and go between builds, as the choice between two copies of one method does (row 990). Measured once, on `832f7d0d91`'s code. Detail: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/probe-y.md`, "6. A finding beside the question: the prelude's jars change with any change of the compiler".
## Landed semantics

- F-117 **A compiled mutable variable's cell holds the language's top type, so a mutable variable of arrow type compiles and runs.** The cell holds `fortress.AnyType.Any`, not `FValue`, because a compiled closure is not an `FValue`. The cell's gated tests, `compiler_tests/AtomicTopLevel*Var` and `MutableTopLevelVarInLoop`, run no variable of arrow type. Detail: `compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 4.
- F-118 **A numeral's value reaches the compiled code intact, and the compiled path prints a large `NN32` or `NN64` value unsigned.** A numeral that no place types becomes its default through that type's own coercion, which the checker inserts (`Functionals.scala`, `defaultNumeral`); only a numeral that the checker leaves without a coercion reaches the code generator's fallback, a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by exact bit length (`CodeGen.java`, `forIntLiteralExpr`), and which numerals do is not measured. A folded constant that the coercion desugarer types at a library number type is that type's constant (F-340), and a numeral as written at a number type is its type's coercion folded to a constant or made once for the place (F-347). So on the compiled path `4294967295` and `18446744073709551615` keep their values, as under walk, where they are a `ZZ64` and a `ZZ` (F-74, F-341); an untyped binding of the second is a `ZZ`, its default (F-342). The compiled path prints an `NN32` or `NN64` value above its type's signed half unsigned (F-313; test `compiler_tests/UnsignedPrintingCompiled`). Gated, for the numerals at `ZZ`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, by `compiler_tests/IntLiteralWrapRepairR2`. Detail: `compile-ladder/repair-r2-literal-wrap/REPORT.md`, "The failure-mode question"; `compile-ladder/rung-static-numerals/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why".
- F-119 **The library's scalar extension is eight generic declarations: `+`, `-`, `MIN` and `MAX` between an `Array[\T,I\]` and a scalar `T`, in both orders.** `T` is bounded by `Number` and `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` for `+` and `-`, by `Number` and `StandardMin[\T\]` for `MIN`, and by `Number` and `StandardMax[\T\]` for `MAX`. Gated by `tests/ArrayScalarExtension.fss` and `tests/ArrayOperatorsBesideLibrary.fss`. The second imports the fixture `test_library/ArrayOperatorVocabulary`, which declares two overloads each of `MINMAX`, `+` and juxtaposition over the library's arrays. Walk checks such overloads against the library's only on a cold cache (F-269). So a pass of that test shows that they coexist with the library only if the run started from an empty cache. Detail: `reviews/library-scalar-extension-review.md`, change 1.
- F-120 **A top-level variable imported through an api can be read, assigned and read back on the compiled path.** The checker asks the declaring api whether the name is mutable, and the code generator binds a mutable one to its cell. Gated by `compiler_tests/ExportVarRungX.test`, and the refusal to assign an immutable one by `XXXExportVarRungXFrozen.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`, "What the rung landed".
- F-121 **The team's spelling of `AnyIntegral`'s `comprises` clause, `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]`, stays a comment, and no decision says whether it is a valid clause.** The live clause, which lists `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`, stands (P-44), and the compiled checker accepts it (F-62). The specification lets a listed type hold a `where`-clause variable, at every value of it, and the compiled checker opens such variables, of a `nat`, an `int` or a type (F-146, F-251). As the team wrote it, the clause is ill-formed: past the front end's refusal of such a clause on a trait that declares a coercion (row 831), the compiled checker reports 'Ill-formed type: Integral[\I\] The static argument I does not satisfy the corresponding bound Integral[\I\]', since `where [\I\]` binds `I` without the bound that `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` asks for. With the bound, `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` in place of the list, the checker finds 0 errors in every api of the one library, but the `FortressLibrary` component's overloading and export checks run out of memory at the stages' 4 GB heap (`TypeAnalyzer.ancestors`, `TypeAnalyzer.scala:1032`) and finish clean at 11 GB ('#total 0', '#crash none'). Neither can be reached on `main`, where the clause is not live; no test checks either, and the probe's lifter fix and clause are at the end of its report. Of the team's commented `comprises ... where` clauses, P-151 builds only `AnyList`'s. The comment stays by P-44, which kept it beside the live clause when its `where` form was not built. Whether it becomes live now that the checker opens such variables is an open question, whose default leaves it. Detail: `coordinator/process-engineering/facts-slice-2.md`, "Points for the checker", point 1; `perf-probes/anyintegral-comprises-where/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 5.
- F-122 **`round` on an `RR64` or an `RR32` sends an exact half to the even integer on both paths.** NaN gives 0, and a value beyond the `ZZ64` range saturates to the `ZZ64` bounds. On both paths, a numeral within half an ulp of a tie rounds as its nearest double, not as the rational that it denotes, by P-173's tie reading (P-172; the guard `tests/RoundNearTieNumeral.fss`). The ties are gated under walk by `tests/RoundHalfEvenRungR.fss`, and on the compiled path, for `RR64`, by `library_tests/RR64FunctionsRungF.fss`; the compiled `RR32` ties were observed in a probe of the report. NaN and saturation are gated on neither path: they were observed in the report's walk probe and compiled differential, and read in the code (`(long) Math.rint` in `Float.java:384`, `RR32.java:326` and `simpleDoubleArith.java:132-134`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-round-half-even/REPORT.md`, "What landed" and "Differentials".
- F-123 **A compiled object with no `asString` of its own prints its bare type name, as walk does.** A value whose run-time Java class declares its own `toString`, such as the compiled `RR32`'s, prints by it. Open on the compiled path: through the prelude's `Object`, an object that declares or inherits a zero-argument Fortress member named `toString` overflows the stack when it is printed (row 321), though not through the one library's `Object`, whose `asString` is `self.ilkName`; and `asDebugString` and `asExprString` print differently from walk's, where the specification is silent (row 363). For a string static argument both paths give `Cell[\String\]`, the specification's answer, walk reading a string object at `String` (F-344). For a numeral argument both paths give the numeral's default, the specification's answer: `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\ZZ32\]` (`tests/LanguageTypeInstancesWalk`, `compiler_tests/LiteralDefaultCompiled`; F-341, F-342). Gated by `compiler_tests/DefaultRenderRungS`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-default-rendering/REPORT.md`, "Defects and their homes".
- F-124 **On the compiled path, at or beyond the width of `ZZ32` or `ZZ64`, `LSHIFT` gives 0 and `RSHIFT` the sign; both reverse on a negative count, and `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits.** "The sign" is 0 for a nonnegative value and -1 for a negative one. `ZZ64`'s and `NN64`'s `narrow` to 32 bits keeps the low 32 bits. `<<`, `>>` and `<<<` keep their own rules, and `asZZ32` throws out of range. Negation, absolute value and division overflow only at the minimum value and test exactly for it, so the minimum raises `IntegerOverflow`, and `|0|`, `-0` and `0 DIV -1` answer 0. Addition and subtraction test the sign bits, and multiplication computes the exact product (`Math.multiplyExact` on `ZZ64`, a range-checked 64-bit product on `ZZ32`). So these raise `IntegerOverflow` on every overflow, and a zero factor answers 0. `ZZ`'s `<<<` raises a catchable `IntegerOverflow` on a shift that it cannot represent (row 386). Gated by `compiler_tests/IntSemanticsRungB.fss`, and for addition and subtraction by the team's `library_tests/Integer3.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-compiled/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-125 **Under `walk`, at or beyond the width of `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` or `NN64`, `LSHIFT` gives 0 and `RSHIFT` the sign; both reverse on a negative count, and `ZZ`'s `shift` computes ⌊x·2^k⌋.** It builds P-69. "The sign" is 0 for a nonnegative value and -1 for a negative one. `ZZ`'s `shift(x, k)` is ⌊x·2^k⌋. A nonzero value shifted by a positive count beyond 2^31 - 1 raises a catchable `IntegerOverflow`, as does any result that the JVM's `BigInteger` cannot hold; zero shifted stays zero. The compiled path declares no `shift` (F-126). Gated by `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` sections 4.3 and 4.4.
- F-126 **`ZZ`'s functional method `shift` reserves the name `shift` in every program under walk, and not on the compiled path, whose prelude declares no `shift`.** The `fortress-repo` skill gives the general rule (`references/library.md`). So the library's parameters that `shift` would shadow are named `amount`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/JUDGE.md` section 3; the renames, its `REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-128 **Under `walk`, the interpreter converts by coercion at its three kinds of type check.** They are a parameter, a varargs parameter included; an overloaded call that no declaration fits without coercion, which walk then dispatches again; and a typed binding or assignment. Walk chooses the coercion by the run-time value (P-59). Not converted, as measured: a value other than a numeral at a declared return (row 387; a numeral converts there, F-341), a coercion with its own static parameter, unless it is a numeral coercion (row 513), and an overloaded function's tuple parameter or a tuple-typed field (row 395). Not converted, by the code, and not measured: a varargs or keyword element of the specification's tuple coercion, and its arrow coercion. Gated by `tests/Coercion*RungC.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-interp-coercion/REPORT.md` sections 1, 5 and 9.
- F-129 **A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`, and a program whose sizes are known at compile time loads, dispatches and runs compiled, apart from the open cases below.** It builds P-41. Each size value, such as the 3 of `Vec[\3\]`, has one descriptor; in a run-time subtype test, it is a supertype only of an equal size. A size read as a value is a `ZZ32` that the class loader writes in: `FZZ32.make` of an `int`, or, beyond 31 bits, `FZZ32.makeSize` of its digits, a `java.lang.Error` at run time that no `catch` sees (row 962; `runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:225-237`, by reading). Closures and tasks capture a size as a free static parameter (F-135). A size made from a number known only at run time does not run compiled: `tests/NatReflectTest.fss` stops at load (row 307). Two findings bear on any binding that both paths share. First, a helper raises a Fortress exception by naming a class of the compiled prelude, such as `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$IntegerOverflow`. Walk has no such class: its loader of a `builtinPrimitive` helper translates the raise into the library's exception (F-299), but through a written `import java` walk ends the run with a `FortressImplementationError`, unless the probe's patch for gap 5 (`gap5-helper-raise.patch`) translates the raise. Second, by reading, a helper whose parameters or results are compiled-path classes, such as `FZZ32Vector`, cannot take walk's values. The probe's closure converts only Java's numbers, booleans, strings and `BigInteger`, and the helper classes had 50 such parameters or results when read once with `javap`, before `nativeHelpers/simpleIntLiteralArith.java` was deleted; walk's loader refuses at load a binding whose declared type no Java type carries (F-299). Detail: `perf-probes/prelude/natives-shape.md` section 1 (the gaps and walk's half); `perf-probes/prelude/natives-binding-probe.md` section 1 (the compiled half; its section 2 measures the `import java` form, which P-58 did not take); `compile-ladder/rung-natives-compiled/SKEPTIC.md`, "My programs, old against new".
- F-181 **The code generator compiles a function, method, object or trait declaration that carries a `where` clause in its own header, emitting nothing for the clause, and refuses every function or method with a contract (row 701).** The clause's constraints are the checker's. A trait's or object's contract does not reach the refusal: the disambiguator drops it (row 781); F-255 says how each path reads a `where` clause on an `extends` entry (row 774). Walk checks a function's `requires` clause and raises `CallerViolation`. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet", gives the refusal and the constructs that the code generator has no case for; an array comprehension has no case either. A local function compiles as a closure, except in the four forms that F-320 names. A trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size, of `NatParam`'s shape, compiles; a call that opens its value to the size fails verification (row 307). Where a generic type that such a clause lists gives a member's body, the code generator crashes first (row 812). A function's or method's own clause that introduces a `where`-clause variable compiles, and the compiled call dies with `NoClassDefFoundError` (row 867). Tests: `compiler_tests/WhereBoundFunctionCompiled`, `WhereBoundMethodCompiled`, `WhereBoundObjectCompiled`, `WhereBoundTraitMethodCompiled`, `ComprisesWhereFunctionalMethodCompiled`; `XXXFunctionContractCodeGeneration`; the `XXXNatOpenRun` pair; the `XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled` pair. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-codegen-where/REPORT.md`, sections 1, 2 and 5.
- F-182 **Both paths refuse a `type` alias, a `test` declaration of the form `test Id[gens] = Expr`, and a `property` declaration, in the index builder that both paths run (`scala_src/typechecker/IndexBuilder.scala:187-189`).** At top level, each stops its component with `** bug! Not yet implemented:` and the declaration's kind, such as `TestDecl`: the type alias in row 18, the `test` declaration in row 121, and the `property` declaration in row 122. Inside an object, a `property` declaration stops with an uncaught `java.lang.Error`, and a `test` declaration does not parse. The rows observe walk. On the compiled path, the type alias was observed to stop in the same way (`explorations/aliases-units-report.md:98-101`); the other two forms are by reading, from the shared index builder. A function with the `test` modifier is another form, and it runs under `fortress test` (row 120 records it working).
- F-183 **The compiled path's only array-like types are `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`, two hand-written Java classes declared only in its prelude and absent from the specification.** Each element access is boxed. No gated test makes or indexes a `ZZ32Vector` at run time. Gated tests make a `StringVector`, store two strings in it with `putValue` and assert its rendering (`compiler_tests/DefaultRenderRungS`), and read `args`, which is one (`Compiled2`). Passed to a generic object's constructor, either type fails at load: its descriptor class is `RTTIv`, where stamped code asks for `RTTIc`. Row 408 and `compiler_tests/XXXVecCtorLoad` hold this for a `ZZ32Vector`; the probe measured a `StringVector` too. A native helper cannot take a Java array, since the wrapper generator skips such methods. Detail: `compiler-probes/vectors/vectors.md` sections 1, 3 (step 9), 6 and 7.
- F-184 **A generic object referenced without its static arguments is a static error on the compiled path, and the checker never consults the expected type for it.** `b: Box[\ZZ32\] = Box` fails as an ill-formed type, and a bare `Empty` as an argument or a field's default as an internal error, `T is not in the kind env`. Walk fails on both. Writing the static argument avoids both. So a bare `Nothing` compiles only against the compiled prelude's own `Nothing` (row 331, P-90). Detail: `compiler-probes/maybe-inference/inference.md`.
- F-185 **The suites run two corpora ported by hand, and no test compares the two paths on one program.** `tests/` shares no file name with `compiler_tests/`, and its 11 names shared with `other_compiler_tests/` are other programs. `fortress.unittests.noopt=true` in `default_repository/configuration` turns off the bytecode optimizer's tests. `TransactionJUTest`'s multi-threaded half is commented out. By the map's one count, 121 `.fss` files in the suites' directories run in no test, and some directories are orphaned. Detail: `coordinator/map/test-coverage.md` sections A.1, A.4 and C.1.
